repository.name: voltrl
repository.title: VoltRL Arbitrage Evidence Lab
repository.description: Audit battery-arbitrage assumptions with finite-state benchmarks, chronological protocols & reproducible model evidence.
repository.summary: VoltRL compares finite-state battery policies under synthetic prices and a documented historical day-ahead protocol. The browser isolates a generic friction calculation before the native inventory, aging, and information constraints.
repository.audience: Energy-market researchers and developers learning to compare battery policies without information leakage.

model.equation: spread = b + 12 sin(2πt/12) + 5 sin(2πt/5); edge = spread − fees − slippage; P&L = notional · edge/10000.
assumptions: All prices, spreads, and returns are synthetic; no exchange or trading API is connected.
P&L is one hypothetical opportunity at the selected time, not accumulated realized performance.
Execution latency, inventory, liquidity, funding, and exchange risk are omitted.
All spreads and notional values are invented; no OPSD file or native benchmark output is loaded by the browser.
The native project uses finite-state MDP/dynamic-programming methods; this page neither trains deep-RL agents nor counts rainflow cycles.
The browser omits battery inventory, terminal valuation, market fees beyond the explicit toy inputs, and causal decision timing; it offers no trading-performance conclusion.
model.introduction: This normalized USD/basis-point screen is not VoltRL’s energy-market reward or policy solver. It illustrates why a gross opportunity and its costs must be separated before inspecting the native MWh, efficiency, degradation, and information protocol.

modules.title: Separate a gross spread from a net result
modules.objective: Reconcile a normalized hypothetical opportunity before comparing policies.
steps: Read VoltRL’s stated battery, reward, and information conventions.
Apply a 40 bps base spread, 10 bps fees, 5 bps slippage, and 10,000 USD notional.
At time zero, calculate net edge and scenario P&L; identify the native energy-market variables absent from this arithmetic.
modules.reflection: Why must a result in basis points of notional not be compared directly with currency per MWh or an annual battery profit?

modules.title: Find the break-even boundary
modules.objective: Show how costs can remove an apparent gross opportunity.
steps: Keep base spread at 40 bps and notional at 10,000 USD.
Raise fees to 25 bps and slippage to 15 bps, predict the time-zero result, then inspect the final synthetic time.
Read the native degradation-cost conventions and explain why fees, efficiency losses, and aging are separate quantities.

checkpoints.label: The opening opportunity is exactly break-even

modules.reflection: Which costs are modeled natively, and which remain omitted from the price-taking benchmark?

modules.title: Protect the information boundary
modules.objective: Explain why a policy may not use future realized prices just because a plot displays them.
steps: Reduce base spread to 20 bps while retaining the 25/15 bps cost assumptions.
Inspect the time-zero and 24-hour points; remember these are two separate hypothetical opportunities, not accumulated P&L.
Read the historical 24-hour block protocol and distinguish a causal schedule from the perfect-foresight upper bound.

checkpoints.label: Opening net edge is negative 20 bps
Final scenario P&L under the declared costs

modules.reflection: What timestamp and training/holdout checks would reveal an optimistic result caused by information leakage?

modules.title: Assemble a reproducible benchmark claim
modules.objective: Tie a comparison to its data source, source revision, protocol, and metric definitions.
steps: Apply a 55 bps base spread, 20 bps fees, 10 bps slippage, and 20,000 USD notional.
Run to 24 hours and export the synthetic assumptions without describing the result as an energy-market backtest.
Read the OPSD provenance record and the result-bundle audit; list the checks needed before quoting a native policy comparison.

checkpoints.label: Declared fees and slippage total 60 USD

modules.reflection: How would you report a perfect-foresight benchmark, a synthetic policy result, and an audited historical result without conflating their evidential strength?
